I've been into metal working recently due to a task at my job. I mirror polish certain pieces to prep them for operation. Due to this I was inspired to dabble into knife sharpening since my knives in the kitchen were getting dull. I bought a simple kitchen sharpener tool, and it worked okay for slicing meat or vegetables but I wanted more. I tried honing one of my pocket knives first by mirror polishing it to get it dull then by honing it on whatever I had. I wanted to get it sharp enough to shave with. I even pulled out an old leather belt and tried stropping it. Needless to say it COULD cut hair but not good at all.

I bought a straight razor and tried it out yesterday. It came with a two piece strop. I also ordered a 5000/10000 grit waterstone which I haven't touched yet. I stropped the razor about 100 strokes each side using the finer side of the leather. I had a very hard time shaving, it was my first time. Holding it felt awkward, and I felt like I was scratching the hair off instead of smoothly shaving it. My chin and jaw I had the hardest time with, there is a steep angle and it was hard for me to maneuver around. In the end I cut myself up pretty rough, and the shave quality was as if I used a 2 blade bic disposable.

This razor wasn't really shave ready. It was a cheaper one, made in china. I have my stone and I'm thinking to sharpen this myself, maybe even dull and resharpen that previous knife as well. I'm also thinking I can take these to a local shop to ask them to hone it if worst comes to worst. Another issue is that I didn't know what I was doing with the razor for my shave. I've seen some videos online, especially Lynn Abrams. Do you guys have any advice on this situation? Should I tap out with this razor and buy more expensive one? What about for shaving technique, what can I do to improve?
Need some straight razor shaving advice

Get a few grit diamond stones and good compound. I don't shave with anything besides a safety razor, but my chisels and planes are very very sharp. There's a few good youtube videos on sharpening, honing, and stropping. I can't know your razor, but if it has one flat side, make sure it's flat.

Get a better razor, either Japanese or Sheffield steel will hold a honed edge better then chineseium. Get a bottle of fine carbide powder and dust the strop (tiny tiny bit). Hand sharpening and honing are like welding, you have to do a few miles of it before you get good. Try short strokes while shaving with lots of rinsing so you don't clog the edge. Other then that you are just going to have to figure it out. Using a safety razor might be a better option, a year's blades are like $5.

'not shave ready'

So, here's a thing about razors: They are extremely shep edged, think more so than a scalpel. You can't just stroke a not shave ready blade on leather, because that is to hone the blade, not sharpen it. If you look at it under a microscope, you'd see it still looked serrated. That's what the leather fixes, like those steels they give you in every knife block kit.

So, I'd recommend starting over honestly. Find a quality shave ready razor, I think the guys at Harry's have some pretty decent ones. When you get it, they should have prep instructions. Follow those, and look up some videos on technique. This is not something you can just pick up and use, you've gotta learn and practice but it's the best shave you'll get.

Good luck!

First of all I don't have the skills to do what you're trying to do. Honing an edge on a straight razor takes some time to learn. It is the finest edge you will ever try to put on a blade and I didn't want to buy the stones to do it. You can buy pre-honed blades from people who have those skill, but if your goal is to develop those skills then I'd suggest buying some old straight razors from back when everybody used them. You can try ebay or antique shops or whatever, they'll probably have broken scales (the handle part) ans need a complete restoration, but as long as the blade edge isn't pitted with rust you'll be able to polish it up and put a good edge on it. Back in the day there were whole industries set up to provide the world with these blades. Solingen Germany is a name you'll see a lot, some knife companies are still located there. J.A. henckels is an old razor company that still around and makes kitchen knives.

The purpose of getting an old blade is you'll KNOW the quality of the steel is what it needs to be for a proper shave. Anything modern and you might be getting chinezium that won't be able to hold as fine of an edge as you need to put on it to get a proper shave. I want to direct you to a message board called Badger and Blade where they talk about a lot of stuff related to wetshaving and have subforums dedicated to restoring old blades. It's been around for like 15 years so they have a lot of guides and old posts about stuff that will help you out.

I can hone a tuna can lid on a dirty boot and shave with it just fine, so it's not the blade. The trick to the straight razor is to shave with the grain, with a very slight angle with edge pointing in the direction of travel. I also pinch the blade at about it's midpoint rather than trying to hold the handle. This lets the blade float around the contours better. It also helps to have a good shaving cream, and if you apply it a couple minutes before you start, it softens the hairs up a bit and makes it a lot easier.

Sharpening/honing wise, make sure to lift at the end of the stroke, right before your wrist has the tendency to roll the edge. Sharpening is where you set your edge. Stropping actually just pulls the little jagged remnants off for a smoother cut. For anything but shaving, a non stropped blade will actually cut a little better due to the tiny serrations left behind.
